policy: Material legal references must be traced to current official instruments. A cited source or captured hash does not establish that dependency status is current. Preserve national wording; editorial alerts belong here.

evidence: Official amendment references confirm NN 85/15 and 69/22; verify consolidated procedure, access to case files, exemptions, deadlines and Commissioner appeal.
Current MUP index checked 2026-10-19 lists the EEA Act chain NN 66/19, 53/20, 144/20 and 114/22; it does not provide consolidated wording.

Accepted EEA Act NN 66/19 Article 2 expressly states that the Act transposes Directive 2004/38. Articles 1(1), 1(3) and 1(4) define national scope and treatment of EEA, Swiss and specified Croatian-national family cases.

Article 1(4) does not, by itself, resolve a third-country-national family member returning with a Croatian citizen after free movement in another Member State. Map Directive cross-border scope and relevant EU case law before assigning the Foreigners Act route.

The current MVEP family page embeds an obsolete HTTP EUR-Lex URI for the Directive; use the official ELI locator for dependency monitoring and retain the stale in-page link as an extraction/link-quality finding.
NN 86/21 article 1 refers to Regulation (EU) 2019/1157; the CJEU declared that regulation invalid in C-61/22 and maintained its effects pending replacement.

Regulation (EU) 2025/1208 Article 7 requires the card format and a standardized code in data field [10]. Article 8 applies only to residence cards for non-EU family members: cards failing Article 7 generally cease at expiry or 3 August 2026; cards failing Article 7 but meeting ICAO minimum security standards and Annex points (c) and (g) conditions may continue to expiry or 3 August 2031; cards without minimum ICAO security or a functional MRZ are not valid. The card-specific conditions cannot be inferred from the blank Form 11b image.

On 2026-10-25 the four official NN 86/21 Form 4b/11b images were inspected at native dimensions and retained unchanged. They are blank specimen layouts, not proof of actual issued card encoding or security features.

NN 86/21 Article 27a(5) and Regulation 2025/1208 Article 7(2) in the official Croatian text prescribe the same standardized Article 10 code. The blank Form 11b specimen does not establish that the actual issued card carries it in data field [10], or demonstrate the current card’s format/security.

The MUP Propisi index checked 2026-10-25 lists EEA rule chain NN 107/20, 148/20, 86/21 and 155/22. The current MUP forms index lists application/registration forms 1b, 2b, 3b and 6b, not card specimens. MUP guidance updated 2025-10-09 describes issue process but does not show the post-transition card.
review_questions: Obtain or identify an official MUP specimen or other authoritative evidence of the card actually issued after 3 August 2026, including the standardized code’s placement in data field [10].
Verify Article 8 transition treatment only from the actual card’s ICAO/MRZ and Annex-condition evidence; do not infer it from the blank specimen.
Confirm the personal scope of Article 6 for the EEA nationalities covered by Form 4b before making a nationality-wide conclusion.
Keep the CJEU C-61/22 invalidity/effects analysis separate from the current-card format check.

dependencies.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2025/1208, Articles 7 and 8; judgment C-61/22; Croatian EEA Regulation amendment NN 86/21, Articles 1, 5, 10 and 11
evidence: The Croatian amendment attaches 2021 Form 4b and Form 11b specimens. Regulation (EU) 2025/1208 Article 6 sets minimum information for Union-citizen residence documents; Articles 7 and 8 concern non-EU family-member cards and their format/transition. Article 8 includes a conditional 2031 phase-out route for some cards that fail Article 7 but meet specified security conditions.

The Croatian-language Article 7(2) standardized Article 10/20 code matches the wording prescribed by NN 86/21 Article 27a(5). Form 2b is an application, not a residence-card specimen. The blank Form 11b image does not establish actual issuance, code placement in data field [10], or Article 8 transition eligibility.
review_questions: Verify the actual current Form 4b and Form 11b card issuance with authoritative evidence; compare Form 4b to Article 6 only within confirmed personal scope.
For Form 11b, verify the standardized code in data field [10] and the format/security features; use Article 8 transition classes only when actual-card conditions are evidenced.
Record an evidence-based conclusion without altering the source’s original Croatian text.

dependencies.instrument: General Administrative Procedure Act NN 47/09, 110/21; Administrative Disputes Act NN 36/24; Constitutional Court decision NN 39/26 concerning Article 169(2)
evidence: Existing official sources located; compare application, supplementation, hearing, service, delay/omission, appeal, court deadlines, suspensive effect, and interim relief.

Accepted source records are now available for the General Administrative Procedure Act chain NN 47/09 + 110/21 and the Administrative Disputes Act NN 36/24. ZUS Articles 3 and 12 expressly cover claims against decisions, conduct and failure to act/decide within a statutory deadline. The exact application and remedy path for each EEA-family decision remains unmapped.

Official Ministry source identifies the current GAPA chain; official Croatian courts law listings identify ZUS NN 36/24. Neither listing substitutes for a consolidated text, exhaustive dependency scan or remedy crosswalk.

The Constitutional Court decision NN 39/26 was reviewed on 2026-10-21. It starts constitutional review and repeals ZUS/24 Article 169(2), a transition rule for proceedings where a hearing had closed before 1 July 2024. The decision is relevant to transitional cases; no effect is inferred for ordinary current EEA procedures.
review_questions: Map GAPA and ZUS provisions to EEA-family applications, service, decision time limits, challenge to silence, appeal exhaustion, interim measures and execution.
Compare each general provision in procedural-crosswalk.md with the current EEA Act/regulation and visa/Foreigners Act route before treating any immigration issue as mapped.
For any proceeding within the old-law transition, verify the decision’s exact effective timing and application to the case; do not generalize it to current residence applications.

evidence: Official NN 68/18 text states it transposes Directive (EU) 2016/680. Determine processing purposes and controller for each VIS/SIS right or complaint; do not substitute GDPR rules without a purpose check.

The MUP page and its three linked PDFs cite Regulations (EU) 2018/1861 and 2018/1862, including Articles 53 and 67. The page separately contains a 2018/1061 typo; the forms show the correct identifiers.

On 2026-10-25 the official NN 68/18 page was identified by title, issue metadata, item 1391 and ELI. Articles 1–3 state the law-enforcement purposes, LED transposition, scope and exclusions; selected rights and oversight text in Articles 15–17 and 41–44 was reviewed. This establishes the original enactment and selected text only; amendment/currentness, processing-purpose classification, controller competence and VIS/SIS route remain unresolved.
Listed or cross-referenced in official Croatian visa sources; amendments and application date to be checked.

On 2026-10-25 the original NN 92/21 Visa System Decree was checked by link. Articles 1–2 describe the national visa-system/means subject matter and its stated implementation of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806; current amendment status, present amounts and issue-specific EEA-family effect remain open.

dependencies.instrument: Regulation (EC) No 767/2008 (VIS), Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), and law-enforcement data rules
evidence: MUP/MVEP indexes list Croatian VIS instruments; differentiate GDPR-controlled processing from law-enforcement processing and trace controller/complaint routes.
The live MVEP page and linked form cite the VIS Regulation (EC) No 767/2008 and GDPR rights; the form requests access, correction and deletion, while the page also mentions restriction.

On 2026-10-25 the official NN 36/13 VIS regulation and NN 105/17 amendment were checked by link. Articles 35–37 of the original text state selected notice, access/correction/deletion and AZOP-oversight provisions; Article 21(3) was changed by NN 105/17. This does not determine current effect after later EU VIS rules or classify a specific operation under GDPR versus LED.
MVEP official visa-regulations index lists Visa Code and domestic rules; exact Article 32/appeal relationship and family-member derogations require review.

dependencies.instrument: Administrative Fees Act NN 115/16, 114/22; Tariff NN 156/22, 130/25; Directive 2004/38/EC Article 5(2); EU Charter Article 47
evidence: Administrative Fees Tariff item 30 as amended by NN 130/25 sets €130 for an appeal against refusal, annulment or revocation of a visa and specified visa-based stay decisions. Current MVEP appeal guidance states €130 or USD 150.71 and a 15-day deadline, 60-day decision period, and 30-day administrative-court route.

Directive 2004/38 Article 5(2) requires a necessary entry visa for a qualifying family member to be issued free of charge. The Commission’s 2023 free-movement notice describes that rule as applying to visa issuance and says the Directive does not set other visa-issuance procedures. Those sources do not resolve whether or how a Croatian appeal fee may apply to a qualifying family-member case.

Keep the initial visa fee and the appeal fee analytically separate. Compatibility, any exemption/waiver, language and filing conditions, and effective access to review under the Visa Code and Charter Article 47 remain open. Preserve the Croatian tariff wording.
review_questions: For a fee question, review the current official tariff, enabling Act, MVEP route, and relevant Foreigners Act provisions. Retaining captures or hashes is optional; check only the provisions that affect the fee or remedy question.
Determine whether tariff item 30 applies to an appeal by a qualifying Directive 2004/38 family member and whether an exemption, waiver or refund exists.
Review the 15-day deadline, Croatian-language rule and exception, filing channel and 30-day court route against the applicable Visa Code, Directive and Charter requirements.
Do not infer that a free visa issuance makes a later appeal free; do not infer compatibility from the tariff text alone.

dependencies.instrument: Court Fees Act NN 118/18, 51/23; Tariff NN 37/23 (transition only), 50/26; Administrative Disputes Act NN 36/24; Free Legal Aid Act NN 143/13, 98/19; secondary legal-aid compensation regulation NN 142/25.
evidence: Court Fees Tariff NN 50/26, effective 1 June 2026, sets €110 for an administrative claim and €140 for appeals and specified High Administrative Court filings. Article 2 preserves NN 37/23 rates for administrative disputes commenced before 1 June 2026.

Court Fees Act Article 22(1) says court fees in an administrative dispute are payable only if the court rejects the claim or dismisses the action. The tariff amounts therefore must not be described as an up-front fee to lodge every initial claim without checking the Act and procedural context.
The risk of later fees/costs, appeals, legal-aid eligibility, waiver/suspension, and effective access remain open for the relevant applicants and case types.

Accepted NN 142/25 is a year-specific 2025 provider-compensation regulation; Article 7 prices lawyer work in administrative disputes. It is not an applicant eligibility or court-fee exemption rule. The 2026 annual successor remains unresolved.
review_questions: Capture and compare NN 50/26, NN 37/23 transition terms, the Court Fees Act and amendment, and current procedural provisions.
Map when each fee becomes due, including claim, appeal, decision and High Administrative Court stages; distinguish filing cost from outcome-based liability.
Verify current legal-aid eligibility, waiver/suspension procedure and timing for applicants in relevant residence or visa cases.
Assess actual cost exposure and effective remedy in the relevant case type; do not assume either that all court access is prepaid or that outcome-based fees are immaterial.
Trace the budgetary-base definition to the current annual budget-execution statute and flag practical guidance that still displays kuna.
Resolve the annual 2026 provider-compensation instrument status against a complete Official Gazette record; keep it open if publication cannot be established.

dependencies.instrument: Free Legal Aid Act NN 143/13, 98/19; State Budget Execution Act for 2026 NN 152/25
evidence: Accepted Free Legal Aid Act Article 4(15) ties the budgetary base to the annual budget-execution statute; Article 14(1) uses one base per household member monthly and 60 bases for assets; Article 19(3)(b) uses half a base for full-scope aid.
Accepted amendment NN 98/19 changes specified provisions but not Articles 4(15), 14 or 19.

Accepted State Budget Execution Act NN 152/25 Article 39(2) sets the 2026 base at EUR 441.44 and Article 72 makes the Act effective 1 January 2026. EUR 26,486.40 (60 bases) and EUR 220.72 (half a base) are calculations from the statutory formula.
The Ministry of Finance 2026 page links NN 152/25; a bounded exact-title Gazette search found no amending act as of 2026-10-19. Recheck on later amendment evidence and for the next annual budget act.
MPUDT practical conditions page still displays old kuna values; retain it as a stale comparator and do not quote those values as current.
review_questions: Verify whether EU/EEA family members qualify under the foreign-national categories in Article 5 for the specific residence or visa-remedy proceeding; do not infer entitlement from the statute title.
Reconcile the legal-aid procedure, court-fee waiver and provider routes against accepted primary law and current Ministry forms.
Check the annual 2026 provider-compensation regulation status; the 2025 provider tariff does not set applicant eligibility or court-fee exemption.
Check the next annual budget-execution act before carrying the 2026 base into 2027.
